newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian Solvay H1 1997 profit seen flat.
newsitem.headline: Belgian Solvay H1 1997 profit seen flat.

text.p: Belgian chemicals company Solvay will report flat to slightly higher first half 1997 earnings which are unlikely to affect the company's share price unless the second half outlook looks bad, analysts said.
Solvay is due to announce first half 1997 results after Thursday's close of trade on the Brussels bourse.
In early afternoon trade on Wednesday, Solvay's share was down 2.09 percent at 23,375 Belgian francs.
"The first half will be about the same as in 1996. Results in some sectors will be worse than at the beginning of 1996, results in others better," BBL analyst Georges Piron said.
"I expect a modest increase in first half profit, however I suspect that it won't have any influence on (Solvay's share) price performance," CSFB analyst Penny Tattersall said.
"All the good news is in the price," Piron agreed.

Solvay reported a first half 1996 net profit of 6.0 billion Belgian francs, or 690 francs a share, down from 8.3 billion francs in the same 1995 period. Full year earnings were 13.6 billion francs, including a 2.1 billion franc gain on the sale of its animal health products business, or 1,587 francs a share.

According to 21 analysts polled by Edinburgh Financial Publishing for Reuters 3000, full year 1997 earnings are expected to be around 1,403 francs a share. The range of expectations was 1,336 to 1,965 francs.
Tattersall said she expected a first half profit of around 6.2 billion francs after Solvay said earlier this year that earnings in the first four months were slightly up on 1996.

BBL's Piron said the company's alkalis business, which accounted for 29 percent of 1996 sales, had been worse at the beginning of 1996. Caustic soda prices were down about 45/50 percent on a year ago, he estimated.
Peroxygens, Solvay's smallest business unit, were also under pressure, with prices down by more than 50 percent, he said.

Solvay said in June it would merge its alkalis and peroxygens businesses into a new chemicals unit from July 1. Analysts said they would be looking for the company to provide more details on potential cost savings and synergies.

Meanwhile, Piron said Solvay's plastics business, its biggest, and health businesses, its most promising, would probably post growth, although health sales would be lower due to the end-1996 sale of the animal health business.
It was more difficult to assess prospects in its plastics processing business, where higher raw material costs could have squeezed margins but sales had probably risen, he said.
Solvay does not provide a half-year breakdown of sales in its five main sectors.
